title: Forward GO TO that skips a block becomes if/else
legacy:
IF (X .LT. 0.0) GO TO 20
      Y = SQRT(X)
      GO TO 30
   20 Y = 0.0
   30 CONTINUE
notes: A forward GO TO that skips a block is an if/else: the fall-through code is the else branch and the label after both blocks is just the next statement. Before rewriting, confirm that no other statement jumps to labels 20 or 30. A label with several incoming jumps may need the state-machine form instead. Delete labels that nothing references any more.

title: Backward GO TO with a test at the top becomes while
legacy:
I = 1
   10 IF (I .GT. N) GO TO 20
      S = S + A(I)
      I = I + 1
      GO TO 10
   20 CONTINUE
modern:
i = 1
while i <= n:
    s = s + a[i - 1]
    i = i + 1
notes: The exit test at label 10 is negated to form the while condition. Because the index is incremented by an explicit statement (not by a DO), it keeps its value after the loop exactly as in Fortran: n + 1 here, or 1 when n < 1. Do not turn this pattern into a for/range loop if the code after the loop reads I and the loop can also be left early.

title: Backward GO TO with a test at the bottom (repeat-until)
notes: The body always runs at least once, so a plain 'while cond:' would be wrong; use 'while True' with a break on the negated condition. Write the negation as 'not (...)' rather than flipping the operator: with NaN operands 'x <= eps' and 'not (x > eps)' differ.

title: GO TO out of a DO loop (search with found index)
legacy:
DO 10 I = 1, N
         IF (A(I) .EQ. KEY) GO TO 20
   10 CONTINUE
      IFOUND = 0
      GO TO 30
   20 IFOUND = I
   30 CONTINUE
notes: Leaving a DO by GO TO becomes break, and the code that follows the loop normally becomes the for/else branch or an initial value. After a normal exit the Fortran index is 1 + max(n, 0), i.e. n + 1 (the else branch restores it, since Python stops at n); after an early exit it keeps the current value, which is what break gives. Drop the else branch if I is not read after the loop.

title: GO TO the loop's terminal CONTINUE means continue
legacy:
DO 10 I = 1, N
         IF (A(I) .LE. 0.0) GO TO 10
         S = S + LOG(A(I))
   10 CONTINUE
notes: A jump to the terminal statement of the enclosing DO ends only the current iteration, so it is continue. In nested loops, continue applies to the loop that owns that label; a jump to the label of an outer loop from inside an inner loop needs a flag, a break plus a continue, or a helper function.

title: Irreducible GO TO flow becomes a label variable and while True
legacy:
IF (MODE .EQ. 1) GO TO 20
   10 CALL STEPA(X)
      IF (X .GT. 1.0) GO TO 30
   20 CALL STEPB(X)
      IF (X .LT. 0.0) GO TO 10
   30 CONTINUE
notes: Here the cycle 10-20 can be entered at either label, so no nesting of if and while reproduces it. Emit one block per label, in source order, as sequential ifs (not elif) so that falling off the end of a block runs the next one; set label and continue for a jump, break to leave. STEPA and STEPB assign X, so each returns the new X. Walk every GO TO once to check the table.

title: Several GO TO jumps to one error label become early returns
legacy:
SUBROUTINE SAFEDV(X, Y, Q, IERR)
      IERR = 0
      IF (Y .EQ. 0.0) GO TO 900
      Q = X / Y
      RETURN
  900 IERR = 1
      Q = 0.0
      RETURN
      END
modern:
def safedv(x, y, q, ierr):
    ierr = 0
    if y == 0.0:
        ierr = 1
        q = 0.0
        return q, ierr
    q = x / y
    return q, ierr
notes: A shared exit block at the end of a routine becomes a return in each branch (or a small helper if the block is long). Q and IERR are scalar dummies that are assigned, so every return path must return both, in parameter order, even on paths that never assign them (the incoming value is passed through unchanged).

title: Computed GO TO becomes if/elif with the next statement as else
legacy:
GO TO (10, 20, 30), K
      WRITE(6, *) 'K OUT OF RANGE'
      GO TO 40
   10 X = 1.0
      GO TO 40
   20 X = 2.0
      GO TO 40
   30 X = 3.0
   40 CONTINUE
notes: GO TO (l1, l2, l3), K jumps to the K-th label. If K is less than 1 or greater than the number of labels there is no error: execution simply continues with the statement after the computed GO TO, which is the else branch. Never map K to a list index without this range check (k - 1 would be -1 for k = 0 and silently pick the last element).

title: Computed GO TO whose targets fall through into each other
legacy:
GO TO (10, 20), K
      GO TO 30
   10 A = A + 1.0
   20 B = B + 1.0
   30 CONTINUE
notes: Targets that do not end with a GO TO fall into the following label, so they cannot be separate elif branches: K = 1 runs both increments, K = 2 only the second and any other K none (the GO TO 30 skips both). Use one cumulative condition per block, in source order. Check what each block ends with before choosing between elif and sequential ifs.

title: Computed GO TO inside a loop used as a state machine
legacy:
ISTATE = 1
   10 GO TO (100, 200, 300), ISTATE
      GO TO 900
  100 N = N + 1
      ISTATE = 2
      GO TO 10
  200 N = N * 2
      ISTATE = 3
      GO TO 10
  300 N = N - 3
      ISTATE = 0
      GO TO 10
  900 CONTINUE
notes: The existing state variable is already the dispatch key, so the loop is 'while True' with one branch per label and the out-of-range fall-through (GO TO 900) becomes the else/break. Each block ends by setting ISTATE and jumping back to the dispatch, which the loop does implicitly. With ISTATE = 1 the sequence for N = 0 gives ((0 + 1) * 2) - 3 = -1.

title: Computed GO TO with repeated labels and a MOD selector
legacy:
K = MOD(I, 4) + 1
      GO TO (10, 20, 10, 30), K
      WRITE(6, *) 'NO BRANCH'
      GO TO 40
   10 X = 1.0
      GO TO 40
   20 X = 2.0
      GO TO 40
   30 X = 3.0
   40 CONTINUE
notes: A label may appear several times in the list; merge those positions into one condition. MOD takes the sign of its first argument, so I = -1 gives MOD = -1 and K = 0 (no branch), whereas Python's -1 % 4 is 3 and would wrongly select the last label. The selector in a computed GO TO must be an integer variable, hence the separate assignment to K.

title: ASSIGN / assigned GO TO used as a local subroutine
legacy:
ASSIGN 100 TO IRET
      GO TO 500
  100 ASSIGN 200 TO IRET
      GO TO 500
  200 CONTINUE
      GO TO 600
  500 N = N + 1
      GO TO IRET, (100, 200)
  600 CONTINUE
modern:
def caller(n):
    def bump():
        nonlocal n
        n = n + 1

    bump()
    bump()
    return n
notes: Code reached from several places that returns to the place of call through an assigned label variable is a local subroutine. Make it a nested function (use nonlocal for the variables it assigns), replace each ASSIGN/GO TO pair by a call, and delete the ASSIGN, the assigned GO TO and the dispatch labels. The label list in parentheses only documents the possible targets.

title: ASSIGN used to select a branch later
legacy:
IF (MODE .EQ. 0) ASSIGN 10 TO IGO
      IF (MODE .NE. 0) ASSIGN 20 TO IGO
      GO TO IGO, (10, 20)
   10 R = 1.0
      GO TO 30
   20 R = 2.0
   30 CONTINUE
notes: ASSIGN stores a statement label, not an integer: in Fortran 77 the variable may only be used in assigned GO TO statements or as a format identifier (until it is given an integer value again), never in arithmetic. Give each label a plain integer id in Python and dispatch on it as shown; when the ASSIGN and the GO TO are close together (as here) the variable can be dropped and the original conditions used directly.

title: Arithmetic IF becomes a three-way branch
notes: IF (e) l1, l2, l3 jumps to l1 if e is negative, to l2 if zero, to l3 if positive. The expression is evaluated once, so keep it in a temporary when it is expensive or has side effects. Test the negative case first, then equality with zero, then else. Positive and negative zero both take the middle label.

title: Arithmetic IF with two equal labels is a two-way test
legacy:
IF (N - M) 10, 20, 10
   10 CALL REPORT(1)
      GO TO 30
   20 CALL REPORT(0)
   30 CONTINUE
notes: When two of the three labels coincide the branch collapses: labels (a, b, a) mean 'nonzero versus zero', (a, a, b) mean 'less than or equal to zero versus positive' and (a, b, b) mean 'negative versus not negative'. Read the order of the three labels as (negative, zero, positive) before choosing the comparison.

title: Binary search with a three-way arithmetic IF
legacy:
LO = 1
      HI = N
   10 IF (LO .GT. HI) GO TO 60
      MID = (LO + HI) / 2
      IF (A(MID) - KEY) 20, 50, 30
   20 LO = MID + 1
      GO TO 10
   30 HI = MID - 1
      GO TO 10
   50 IPOS = MID
      GO TO 70
   60 IPOS = 0
   70 CONTINUE
notes: Labels 10 to 30 form a loop, the exit at 50 is a break, and the not-found branch (label 60) is the initial value of IPOS. The midpoint uses integer division; the operands are positive here, but idiv stays correct if they could be negative. The array subscript MID is 1-based, so the element is a[mid - 1].

title: Single-statement logical IF with RETURN, assignment and CALL
legacy:
SUBROUTINE TRACK(A, N, X, XMAX, ICNT)
      REAL A(N)
      IF (N .LE. 0) RETURN
      IF (X .GT. XMAX) XMAX = X
      IF (ICNT .EQ. 0) CALL INIT(A, N)
      RETURN
      END
notes: IF (cond) statement allows one executable statement (assignment, CALL, GO TO, RETURN, STOP, I/O) and becomes a normal if block. Every RETURN, including the early one, returns what the unit returns under the calling convention: here the assigned scalar XMAX (unchanged on the early path), not a bare None. INIT receives A and modifies it in place.

title: DO loop closed by a labeled CONTINUE
legacy:
S = 0.0
      DO 10 I = 1, N
         S = S + A(I)
   10 CONTINUE
notes: The Fortran limit is inclusive, so range stops at n + 1, and the subscript shifts to i - 1. The loop runs max(n, 0) times and does nothing for n < 1. After the loop Fortran leaves I = 1 + max(n, 0); Python leaves i = n, so set i explicitly if it is read afterwards.

title: DO with a negative step
legacy:
DO 20 I = N, 1, -1
         B(N - I + 1) = A(I)
   20 CONTINUE
modern:
for i in range(n, 0, -1):
    b[n - i] = a[i - 1]
notes: With a negative step the inclusive limit 1 becomes the exclusive stop 0 (limit - 1). range(n, 1, -1) is the classic off-by-one that skips I = 1. The trip count is max(0, (1 - n + (-1)) / (-1)) = max(0, n) using truncating division, so n < 1 runs zero times. B(N - I + 1) is b[n - i] after the 1-based shift.

title: DO with a step: trip count and value of the index afterwards
legacy:
K = 0
      DO 30 I = 1, 10, 4
         K = K + 1
   30 CONTINUE
modern:
k = 0
for i in range(1, 11, 4):
    k = k + 1
i = do_final(1, 10, 4)
notes: The loop visits 1, 5 and 9: trip count (10 - 1 + 4) / 4 = 3, so K = 3. After a completed DO the index holds start + trips * step = 13, not the last value 9 that a Python for loop leaves behind. do_final(start, limit, step) returns that value; use it whenever the code after the loop reads the index. do_trips gives the trip count.

title: Zero-trip DO loop and the index afterwards
legacy:
DO 10 I = M, N
         S = S + 1.0
   10 CONTINUE
      K = I
modern:
for i in range(m, n + 1):
    s = s + 1.0
i = do_final(m, n)
k = i
notes: When M > N the body is skipped, but the DO variable is still set to M (start + 0 * step). A Python for loop over an empty range would not even bind i, so assign it after the loop with do_final, which returns start + trips * step. With M = 5, N = 1 this gives K = 5; with M = 1, N = 3 it gives K = 4.

title: DO limit is evaluated once before the first iteration
legacy:
N = 3
      DO 10 I = 1, N
         N = N + 1
         K = K + 1
   10 CONTINUE
modern:
n = 3
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    n = n + 1
    k = k + 1
notes: Start, limit and step are evaluated once and the trip count is fixed, so the body runs 3 times although N grows to 6. Python's range captures its bounds the same way. A rewrite to 'while i <= n' would re-test the changing N and never terminate. Assigning to the DO variable inside the body is not allowed in Fortran 77.

title: DO with a run-time step of unknown sign
legacy:
DO 10 I = ISTART, IEND, ISTEP
         S = S + A(I)
   10 CONTINUE
modern:
for i in do_range(istart, iend, istep):
    s = s + a[i - 1]
notes: When the step is a variable, 'range(istart, iend + 1, istep)' is wrong for a negative step (the stop must be iend - 1) and raises ValueError for a zero step, which Fortran 77 forbids. do_range applies the Fortran trip-count rule for either sign and also works for REAL loop variables.

title: Two nested DO loops closed by one CONTINUE
legacy:
DO 10 I = 1, N
      DO 10 J = 1, M
         A(I, J) = 0.0
   10 CONTINUE
notes: Both DO statements name label 10, so the single CONTINUE ends the inner loop and, immediately after it, the outer one. The textual order of the DO statements gives the nesting: the first is the outer loop. Each loop has its own independent trip count.

title: Shared terminal label on an executable statement
notes: The terminal statement may be an ordinary statement; it belongs to the innermost loop body and is executed once per inner iteration, not again for the outer loop. The inner limit I is evaluated afresh each time the inner loop starts, giving a triangular iteration space (1 trip for I = 1, 2 for I = 2, and so on).

title: Shared terminal label with statements before the inner DO
legacy:
DO 40 I = 1, N
         T = 0.0
         DO 40 J = 1, M
   40    T = T + A(I, J)
      ROWSUM = T
notes: Statements placed between the DO statements, like T = 0.0, belong to the outer body and run once per outer iteration, while the labeled statement is only in the inner body. Nothing may follow the terminal statement inside the outer loop, so the outer loop ends right after the inner one. ROWSUM then holds the sum for the last row only (T is reset every iteration).

title: REAL DO index: trip count is computed up front
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION X
      N = 0
      DO 10 X = 0.0D0, 0.3D0, 0.1D0
         N = N + 1
   10 CONTINUE
notes: Fortran 77 fixes the trip count before the loop as INT((limit - start + step) / step) = INT(0.4 / 0.1) = 4 here (0.0, 0.1, 0.2 and about 0.3). The Python loop 'x = 0.0; while x <= 0.3: ...; x += 0.1' runs only 3 times because 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 is 0.30000000000000004. do_range fixes the count up front and yields start + k * step. Real DO loops were later deleted from the standard and compilers differ at such boundaries, so avoid relying on the endpoint.

title: REAL DO loop rewritten with an integer counter
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION X
      DO 10 X = 0.0D0, 1.0D0, 0.25D0
         S = S + X
   10 CONTINUE
notes: The trip count INT((1.0 - 0.0 + 0.25) / 0.25) = 5 gives x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, and S gains 2.5. The step is exactly representable in binary here, so computing x from the counter equals Fortran's repeated addition. For steps like 0.1 the repeated sums drift from start + k * step in the last bits; do_range and this form both use start + k * step.

title: REAL DO index with a negative step and its final value
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION X
      DO 10 X = 1.0D0, 0.0D0, -0.5D0
         N = N + 1
   10 CONTINUE
notes: Trip count INT((0 - 1 + (-0.5)) / (-0.5)) = 3, so X takes 1.0, 0.5 and 0.0, and N grows by 3. After the loop X holds start + trips * step = -0.5, the value that ended the loop, not the last value 0.0 seen inside the body. do_final computes it; a Python for loop would leave x at 0.0, and at its old value if the loop had zero trips.

title: STOP, STOP with a number and STOP with a message
legacy:
IF (N .LT. 0) STOP 'NEGATIVE N'
      IF (IERR .NE. 0) STOP 2
      STOP
notes: STOP ends the whole program, wherever it is called, so it must be an exception that unwinds through every caller (never sys.exit inside a library function, and never swallowed by a broad except). FortranStop holds a number in .code (None for a plain STOP) or the text in .message. With gfortran STOP n exits with status n, and STOP 'text' prints the text on standard error and exits with status 0.

title: PAUSE statement
legacy:
PAUSE 'MOUNT TAPE 2'
      CALL READIT(N)
modern:
# PAUSE 'MOUNT TAPE 2' (operator interaction, no-op)
readit(n)
notes: PAUSE once suspended the program until the operator resumed it, a feature deleted from later standards. In a converted, non-interactive module it is a no-op; keep the message as a comment so the intent is not lost, and do not insert input() because that would block automated tests.

title: Alternate RETURN n with * dummy arguments
legacy:
SUBROUTINE CHECK(X, Y, *, *)
      IF (X .LT. 0.0) RETURN 1
      IF (X .GT. 100.0) RETURN 2
      Y = SQRT(X)
      RETURN
      END
notes: The * dummies are not Python parameters. RETURN n selects the n-th asterisk (not a label value), and the function reports it as the last element of the returned tuple, 0 for a normal RETURN. Y is an assigned scalar, so it comes first; on the alternate paths it is returned unchanged. With no scalar outputs the function would return the bare int.

title: CALL with *label actual arguments
legacy:
CALL CHECK(A, B, *100, *200)
      WRITE(6, *) B
      GO TO 300
  100 WRITE(6, *) 'NEGATIVE'
      GO TO 300
  200 WRITE(6, *) 'TOO LARGE'
  300 CONTINUE
notes: The labels written *100 and *200 in the CALL are matched to the asterisks by position: the first label is RETURN 1, the second RETURN 2. The caller turns the returned alternate-return number into an if/elif chain and treats 0 as the ordinary fall-through. The label 300 and the GO TO disappear.

title: Asterisk dummies mixed with ordinary arguments
legacy:
SUBROUTINE FINDK(A, N, KEY, *, K, *)
      REAL A(N)
      DO 10 K = 1, N
         IF (A(K) .EQ. KEY) RETURN 1
   10 CONTINUE
      RETURN 2
      END
notes: Asterisks may sit anywhere in the dummy list; they are dropped from the Python parameters while K, an assigned scalar, stays in its place and is returned before the alternate-return number. RETURN 2 is the second asterisk. K is also the DO index, so after the loop completes it is 1 + max(N, 0) and must be set explicitly before the second return.

title: ENTRY points that share saved variables
legacy:
SUBROUTINE ACCUM(X)
      SAVE TOTAL, COUNT
      DATA TOTAL, COUNT /0.0, 0.0/
      TOTAL = TOTAL + X
      COUNT = COUNT + 1.0
      RETURN
      ENTRY ACRESET
      TOTAL = 0.0
      COUNT = 0.0
      RETURN
      ENTRY ACMEAN(AVG)
      AVG = TOTAL / COUNT
      RETURN
      END
modern:
from types import SimpleNamespace

_accum = SimpleNamespace(total=0.0, count=0.0)


def accum(x):
    _accum.total = _accum.total + x
    _accum.count = _accum.count + 1.0


def acreset():
    _accum.total = 0.0
    _accum.count = 0.0


def acmean(avg):
    avg = _accum.total / _accum.count
    return avg
notes: Each ENTRY becomes its own module-level function with the entry's own dummy arguments, executing from the ENTRY statement to the next RETURN. The variables common to the entries live in one module-level state object with the initial values from DATA. Dummy arguments of an entry exist only for calls through that entry, so each function has only its own parameters.

title: FUNCTION with a second entry name
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION FUNCTION CIRCLE(R)
      DOUBLE PRECISION R, CIRCUM
      CIRCLE = 3.14159265358979D0 * R * R
      RETURN
      ENTRY CIRCUM(R)
      CIRCUM = 2.0D0 * 3.14159265358979D0 * R
      RETURN
      END
notes: In a function the result of each entry is the variable named like the entry (CIRCUM), so the entries are independent functions with the same dummy list here. CIRCUM must be declared DOUBLE PRECISION; left to implicit typing it would be a single-precision REAL. Keep the Fortran name of every entry as a Python function name, because callers use them directly.

title: ENTRY in the middle of the body shares the tail
legacy:
SUBROUTINE DBL2(X, Y)
      X = X * 2.0
      ENTRY DBL1(Y)
      Y = Y * 2.0
      RETURN
      END
modern:
def dbl1(y):
    y = y * 2.0
    return y


def dbl2(x, y):
    x = x * 2.0
    y = dbl1(y)
    return x, y
notes: Calling DBL1 starts execution at the ENTRY statement and runs to the end, so it executes only the tail; DBL2 runs the head and then the same tail. Move the shared tail into its own function (here dbl1 itself) and have the earlier entry call it, passing and re-assigning any scalars it modifies. An ENTRY may not appear inside a DO loop or block IF.

title: COMMON block becomes module-level shared state
legacy:
SUBROUTINE SETUP(N0, H0)
      COMMON /GRID/ N, H
      N = N0
      H = H0
      RETURN
      END
      REAL FUNCTION SPAN()
      COMMON /GRID/ N, H
      SPAN = N * H
      RETURN
      END
modern:
from types import SimpleNamespace

grid = SimpleNamespace(n=0, h=0.0)


def setup(n0, h0):
    grid.n = n0
    grid.h = h0


def span():
    return grid.n * grid.h
notes: One object per COMMON block, created once at module level, with the Fortran member names as attributes; every function reads and writes grid.n, never a plain local n (assigning to a bare name would create a local variable and silently lose the update). Members are not initialised unless a BLOCK DATA does it; zero is the practical default. SETUP has no scalar outputs, so it returns None.

title: COMMON members matched by position, not by name
legacy:
SUBROUTINE INITP
      COMMON /PAR/ NX, NY, DX
      NX = 8
      NY = 4
      DX = 0.5
      RETURN
      END
      REAL FUNCTION WIDTH()
      COMMON /PAR/ M, K, H
      WIDTH = M * H
      RETURN
      END
modern:
from types import SimpleNamespace

par = SimpleNamespace(nx=0, ny=0, dx=0.0)


def initp():
    par.nx = 8
    par.ny = 4
    par.dx = 0.5


def width():
    return par.nx * par.dx
notes: Different program units may declare the same block with different member names; the members are associated by position and storage size. Choose one canonical name per position (here the first declaration) and map the others onto it: M is nx, K is ny, H is dx, so WIDTH() is 8 * 0.5 = 4.0. Verify that the type of each position is the same in every unit.

title: COMMON array seen with different shapes by two units
legacy:
SUBROUTINE FILLW
      COMMON /WORK/ V(10)
      DO 10 I = 1, 10
   10 V(I) = I
      RETURN
      END
      REAL FUNCTION PICK(I, J)
      COMMON /WORK/ B(2, 5)
      PICK = B(I, J)
      RETURN
      END
notes: V(10) and B(2,5) occupy the same 10 storage units, so b must be a view of v: reshape with order="F" on a contiguous 1-D array returns a view (the default C order would pick different elements). Never rebind work.v or work.b afterwards, only assign into them. PICK(2, 3) is element 2 + 2 * 2 = 6 of V, i.e. 6.0.

title: EQUIVALENCE of scalars with array elements
legacy:
REAL A(3), X, Y, Z
      EQUIVALENCE (A(1), X), (A(2), Y), (A(3), Z)
      X = 1.0
      A(2) = 5.0
      Z = X + Y
notes: Equivalenced names share storage, so assigning X changes A(1) and the reverse. A Python float has no identity to alias, so every use of X, Y or Z must be replaced by the matching element of the backing array (X is a[0], Y is a[1], Z is a[2]). After these statements A holds 1.0, 5.0, 6.0.

title: EQUIVALENCE of a vector with a matrix as a view
legacy:
REAL W(100), M(10, 10)
      EQUIVALENCE (W(1), M(1, 1))
      DO 10 I = 1, 100
   10 W(I) = REAL(I)
      S = M(2, 3)
modern:
w = np.zeros(100)
m = w.reshape(10, 10, order="F")
for i in range(1, 101):
    w[i - 1] = float(i)
s = m[1, 2]
notes: M(2,3) is storage element 2 + (3 - 1) * 10 = 22, so S is 22.0. Column-major mapping requires reshape with order="F"; the default C order would make m[1, 2] equal to w[12] (13.0). reshape of a contiguous 1-D array yields a view, so writes through either name are seen by the other; keep it as a view and never copy.

title: EQUIVALENCE of REAL and INTEGER to inspect bits
legacy:
REAL R
      INTEGER I
      EQUIVALENCE (R, I)
      R = 1.0
      IB = IAND(I, 2147483647)
modern:
buf = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.float32)
ibuf = buf.view(np.int32)
buf[0] = 1.0
ib = iand(int(ibuf[0]), 2147483647)
notes: Both default types are 4 bytes in gfortran, so a float32 array and an int32 view of the same buffer reproduce the aliasing; 1.0 has the bit pattern 0x3F800000 = 1065353216. Values read through the other type are processor-dependent in the standard, byte order matters for pairs such as DOUBLE PRECISION with two INTEGERs, and the sizes must match the default kinds.

title: EQUIVALENCE aligning the start of one array with the middle of another
notes: EQUIVALENCE (A(1), B(5)) puts A(1) on B(5), so A(i) is B(i + 4) and A(2) is B(6); T is 3.0. A basic slice b[4:] is a view of b, which gives the same aliasing. Do not use fancy indexing or .copy() here, because those would break the sharing.

title: BLOCK DATA initialising a COMMON block
legacy:
BLOCK DATA INIT
      DOUBLE PRECISION PI, E
      COMMON /CONST/ PI, E, NMAX
      DATA PI, E, NMAX /3.14159265358979D0, 2.71828182845905D0, 100/
      END
notes: BLOCK DATA has no executable code; it only gives initial values to named COMMON blocks before the program runs. Put those values into the constructor of the module-level state object so they exist at import time, with no init function that someone must remember to call. Keep the literal digits (3.14159265358979), which are not math.pi.

title: Unnamed BLOCK DATA with an array and a count
legacy:
BLOCK DATA
      COMMON /TAB/ T(4), NT
      DATA T /0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5/, NT /4/
      END
modern:
import numpy as np
from types import SimpleNamespace

tab = SimpleNamespace(t=np.array([0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5]), nt=4)
notes: Only variables of COMMON blocks named in the BLOCK DATA unit can be initialised there; the whole block must be declared (even members that get no value) and a block may be initialised in only one BLOCK DATA unit. If the same block is also declared elsewhere with other member names, the initial values still belong to the shared positions; use one state object for the block and map every unit onto it.

title: DATA with repeat counts for scalars and arrays
modern:
k = np.zeros(5, dtype=int)
a = np.array([1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 3.5])
n = 10
notes: In a DATA list r*c means r copies of the constant c, so 2*3.5 is two elements. The number of constants must match the number of elements. DATA is an initial value, not an assignment executed on each call: if the variable is a local that the routine modifies, it keeps its value between calls (see the SAVE entries).

title: DATA with implied-DO lists
notes: The implied-DO (V(I), I = 1, 10, 2) names elements 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, which are the slice v[0:10:2]; the second list names elements 2, 4, ..., 10. The index I exists only inside the DATA statement and is not a program variable. Elements not named by any DATA statement are undefined in Fortran; zeros are a safe choice.

title: DATA fills a 2-D array in column-major order
notes: Without an implied-DO the constants fill the array in storage order, first subscript fastest: B(1,1)=1, B(2,1)=2, B(1,2)=3, ..., so b[0, 1] is 3.0. The nested implied-DO for C runs J inside I, so values go row by row: C(1,1)=1, C(1,2)=2, C(1,3)=3, C(2,1)=4. Same data, different arrays.

title: SAVE keeps a local counter between calls
legacy:
INTEGER FUNCTION NEXTID()
      INTEGER ICALL
      SAVE ICALL
      DATA ICALL /0/
      ICALL = ICALL + 1
      NEXTID = ICALL
      RETURN
      END
modern:
from types import SimpleNamespace

_nextid = SimpleNamespace(icall=0)


def nextid():
    _nextid.icall = _nextid.icall + 1
    return _nextid.icall
notes: A SAVEd local keeps its value from one call to the next, so it must live outside the function: a module-level state object initialised from DATA (a global statement would also work). The first call returns 1, the second 2, and so on. Because the state persists, tests depend on call order; keep the state in one object so it can be reset between tests.

title: SAVE of an array and a first-call flag
legacy:
REAL FUNCTION ROOTN(I)
      LOGICAL FIRST
      REAL T(50)
      SAVE FIRST, T
      DATA FIRST /.TRUE./
      IF (FIRST) THEN
         DO 10 K = 1, 50
            T(K) = SQRT(REAL(K))
   10    CONTINUE
         FIRST = .FALSE.
      END IF
      ROOTN = T(I)
      RETURN
      END
notes: Both the flag and the lazily filled table are SAVEd, so both are module-level state; the table is allocated once, not rebuilt per call. An index outside 1..50 is an error in Fortran; in Python i = 0 would silently return the last element (index -1), so guard it if callers may pass such values.

title: Local variable that the program assumes is static
legacy:
SUBROUTINE RUNSUM(X, S)
      DATA TOTAL /0.0/
      TOTAL = TOTAL + X
      S = TOTAL
      RETURN
      END
modern:
from types import SimpleNamespace

_runsum = SimpleNamespace(total=0.0)


def runsum(x, s):
    _runsum.total = _runsum.total + x
    s = _runsum.total
    return s
notes: There is no SAVE statement, yet TOTAL is initialised by DATA and modified, and the code clearly relies on it persisting. Under the Fortran 77 standard such a local would become undefined at RETURN, but compilers keep it in static storage (Fortran 90 and later make DATA-initialised variables SAVEd), so legacy programs depend on it. Treat any DATA-initialised local that is also assigned as saved state.

title: Types from the first letter (I-N integer, others real)
legacy:
SUBROUTINE MEAN(X, N, XBAR)
      DIMENSION X(N)
      SUM = 0.0
      DO 10 I = 1, N
         SUM = SUM + X(I)
   10 CONTINUE
      XBAR = SUM / N
      RETURN
      END
notes: No declarations: X, SUM and XBAR are REAL and N and I are INTEGER because of their first letters. SUM / N is a real division (N is converted to real). SUM shadows a Python builtin, so the local is renamed. XBAR is assigned, so it is returned; with N = 0 Python raises ZeroDivisionError where Fortran would produce Infinity or NaN.

title: Assignment to an implicitly INTEGER name truncates
legacy:
NHALF = X / 2.0
      KOUNT = 7
      ITEMP = KOUNT / 2
      RMEAN = KOUNT / 2
modern:
nhalf = int_(x / 2.0)
kount = 7
itemp = idiv(kount, 2)
rmean = float(idiv(kount, 2))
notes: NHALF and KOUNT start with letters I-N and are INTEGER, so storing the real X / 2.0 truncates toward zero (X = -7.0 gives -3, not -4). ITEMP is 3; RMEAN is the REAL 3.0, not 3.5, because KOUNT / 2 is evaluated as an integer division before the conversion. Every undeclared name needs its type derived from its first letter, per program unit.

title: Names that look real but start with I-N
legacy:
MASS = 12.7
      LENGTH = 3
      VOLUME = 2.5 * MASS * LENGTH
modern:
mass = int_(12.7)
length = 3
volume = 2.5 * mass * length
notes: MASS and LENGTH begin with M and L, so they are INTEGER and MASS holds 12, giving VOLUME = 90.0 instead of 95.25. Derive the type from the letter and any IMPLICIT statement rather than from the name's meaning, and note that a misspelled variable silently becomes a new variable with its own implicit type.

title: IMPLICIT DOUBLE PRECISION (A-H, O-Z)
legacy:
IMPLICIT DOUBLE PRECISION (A-H, O-Z)
      X = 0.1
      Y = 0.1D0
      N = 3
      Z = N / 2
modern:
x = float(np.float32(0.1))
y = 0.1
n = 3
z = float(idiv(n, 2))
notes: All names starting with A-H or O-Z are DOUBLE PRECISION while I-N stay INTEGER. The constant 0.1 has no D exponent, so it is still a single-precision constant: X holds 0.10000000149011612, only Y holds the double nearest 0.1. Z is 1.0 because N / 2 is an integer division. IMPLICIT NONE (an extension in Fortran 77) means every name is declared and nothing is inferred.

title: IMPLICIT COMPLEX and IMPLICIT CHARACTER ranges
legacy:
IMPLICIT COMPLEX (Z)
      IMPLICIT CHARACTER*8 (S)
      Z1 = (1.0, 2.0)
      S1 = 'ABC'
modern:
z1 = complex(1.0, 2.0)
s1 = char_assign('ABC', 8)
notes: IMPLICIT assigns a type to every undeclared name beginning with the listed letters: here Z names are COMPLEX and S names are CHARACTER*8, overriding the usual rule for those letters. The statement applies to one program unit only and must precede other declarations (PARAMETER statements may come first).

title: PARAMETER constants and array dimensions
legacy:
INTEGER N
      DOUBLE PRECISION PI, TWOPI
      PARAMETER (N = 10, PI = 3.14159265358979D0)
      PARAMETER (TWOPI = 2.0D0 * PI)
      REAL X(N)
notes: PARAMETER defines compile-time constants that are visible only in the program unit that declares them; define them as local variables at the top of the function, or as module constants when an included file shares them. They can size arrays, and the right side may use earlier parameters. Do not assign to them later.

title: PARAMETER defined by integer division and powers
legacy:
PARAMETER (N = 7)
      PARAMETER (NH = N / 2, NSQ = N ** 2)
      REAL W(NH), G(N, N)
modern:
n = 7
nh = idiv(n, 2)
nsq = ipow(n, 2)
w = np.zeros(nh)
g = np.zeros((n, n))
notes: The constant expressions follow ordinary Fortran arithmetic: NH = 7 / 2 = 3, not 3.5 and not 4, and NSQ = 49. Evaluate them with idiv and ipow rather than with / and **, which would produce floats and break the array sizes.

title: CHARACTER*n assignment pads or truncates
legacy:
CHARACTER*5 A
      CHARACTER*8 B
      A = 'ABCDEFGH'
      B = 'XY'
modern:
a = char_assign('ABCDEFGH', 5)
b = char_assign('XY', 8)
notes: Assigning to a fixed-length CHARACTER variable truncates a longer value on the right (A is 'ABCDE') and pads a shorter one with blanks (B is 'XY' plus six blanks, length 8). A Python str keeps neither the length nor the padding, so every assignment to a CHARACTER*n variable must go through char_assign, and LEN(B) is always 8.

title: CHARACTER comparison ignores trailing blanks
legacy:
CHARACTER*4 A, B
      A = 'AB'
      B = 'AB  '
      IF (A .EQ. B) K = 1
      IF (A .EQ. 'AB') L = 1
      IF (A .LT. 'ABC') M = 1
notes: Fortran compares as if the shorter operand were extended with blanks, so all three tests are true. Python's == is False for 'AB' versus 'AB  ' and the ordering tests differ as well. Use str_eq and str_cmp for .EQ., .NE., .LT. and so on whenever either operand is CHARACTER, even when one side is a literal.

title: CHARACTER*(*) dummy and trailing-blank search
legacy:
INTEGER FUNCTION LENTRM(S)
      CHARACTER*(*) S
      DO 10 N = LEN(S), 1, -1
         IF (S(N:N) .NE. ' ') GO TO 20
   10 CONTINUE
      N = 0
   20 LENTRM = N
      RETURN
      END
modern:
def lentrm(s):
    return len_trim(s)
notes: CHARACTER*(*) takes its length from the actual argument, and LEN(S) includes trailing blanks; the loop finds the last nonblank position (0 for an all-blank string), which is len_trim. A caller that passes an unpadded Python str changes LEN(S), so pad strings to the length the Fortran caller would have declared.

title: CHARACTER*n function result
legacy:
CHARACTER*5 FUNCTION FLAG(K)
      IF (K .GT. 0) THEN
         FLAG = 'YES'
      ELSE
         FLAG = 'NO'
      END IF
      RETURN
      END
notes: The result is a fixed-length CHARACTER*5 value, so the function returns 'YES  ' and 'NO   ' with padding. A test or caller that compares the result with 'YES' must use blank-insensitive comparison (str_eq) or pad the expected value.

title: REAL*8, REAL*4, INTEGER*2 and friends
legacy:
REAL*8 X
      REAL*4 Y
      INTEGER*4 N
      INTEGER*2 K
      COMPLEX*16 Z
      LOGICAL*1 FLAG
modern:
x = 0.0
y = 0.0
n = 0
k = 0
z = 0j
flag = False
notes: The number after * is the size in bytes: REAL*8 is DOUBLE PRECISION, REAL*4 is REAL, COMPLEX*16 is two doubles, INTEGER*4 is the default INTEGER. All map to Python float, int, complex and bool; REAL*4 results carry only about 7 significant digits, which matters for tolerances but not for the type. Narrow integers only matter if the code relies on overflow.

title: INTEGER*2 arithmetic wraps around
legacy:
INTEGER*2 K
      K = 32767
      K = K + 1
notes: On common hardware and compilers the 16-bit result wraps to -32768 (the standard leaves overflow undefined), whereas a Python int just becomes 32768. Reproduce the wrap with a mask only where the program evidently relies on it, such as checksums and hashes; for default 32-bit INTEGER the same idea applies with 2**32 and 2**31.

title: Single-precision constant assigned to a DOUBLE PRECISION variable
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION D, E
      D = 0.1
      E = 0.1D0
      D = 1.0 / 3.0
modern:
d = float(np.float32(0.1))
e = 0.1
d = float(np.float32(1.0) / np.float32(3.0))
notes: A real constant without a D exponent is single precision, and 1.0 / 3.0 is computed in single precision before it is widened: D becomes 0.10000000149011612, then 0.3333333432674408, not the nearest doubles. Writing d = 0.1 or 1.0 / 3.0 in Python changes the 8th digit and fails 1e-12 comparisons against Fortran output. Keep the narrow value unless the author clearly meant double.

title: DBLE only widens; assigning to REAL narrows
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION D, D2
      REAL R
      D = 1.0D0 / 3.0D0
      R = D
      D2 = DBLE(R)
modern:
d = 1.0 / 3.0
r = float(np.float32(d))
d2 = r
notes: R = D rounds to single precision (0.3333333432674408) and DBLE(R) merely widens that rounded value, so D2 differs from D in the 8th digit. Python floats are doubles, so REAL variables whose rounding matters need np.float32 conversion at the assignment; plain float(...) of a double changes nothing.

title: D exponents and forms such as 1D5 and .5D0
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION A, B, C, D, E
      A = 1.0D-3
      B = 2.5D0
      C = 1D5
      D = .5D0
      E = 1.D0
notes: Python has no D exponent, so every D becomes e. A number with an exponent but no decimal point, 1D5, is a DOUBLE PRECISION constant (100000.0D0), not an integer, just as 1E5 is a REAL constant; in Python 1e5 is a float. Forms with a leading or trailing point (.5D0, 1.D0) are also valid Python once the D is replaced (.5e0, 1.e0).

title: E exponent literals are single precision
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION X, Y
      X = 1.0E-3
      Y = 1.0D-3
modern:
x = float(np.float32(1.0e-3))
y = 1.0e-3
notes: 1.0E-3 is a single-precision constant, so X receives 0.0010000000474974513 while Y receives exactly the double 0.001. When translating a program that mixes E and D exponents, keep the distinction instead of mapping both to a Python float literal.

title: COMPLEX arithmetic, CONJG, ABS, REAL and AIMAG
legacy:
COMPLEX Z, W
      Z = (1.0, 2.0)
      W = Z * CONJG(Z) + CMPLX(0.0, 1.0)
      R = ABS(Z)
      X = REAL(W)
      Y = AIMAG(W)
modern:
z = complex(1.0, 2.0)
w = z * z.conjugate() + cmplx(0.0, 1.0)
r = abs(z)
x = w.real
y = w.imag
notes: A complex literal is a pair of real constants in parentheses. W is (5, 1); ABS of a complex is the modulus (square root of 5), REAL and AIMAG give the parts, and CMPLX builds a complex from two reals. Python's operators already follow complex arithmetic, including division.

title: CSQRT, CEXP and complex square roots of negative numbers
legacy:
COMPLEX Z, S, E
      Z = CMPLX(-4.0, 0.0)
      S = CSQRT(Z)
      E = CEXP(CMPLX(0.0, 1.0))
modern:
z = cmplx(-4.0, 0.0)
s = cmath.sqrt(z)
e = cmath.exp(cmplx(0.0, 1.0))
notes: Use cmath for complex arguments: cmath.sqrt(-4+0j) is 2j, while math.sqrt(-4.0) raises ValueError and numpy.sqrt(-4.0) returns nan. The result follows the principal branch. The same applies to generic SQRT, EXP and LOG called with a COMPLEX argument, whereas SQRT of a negative REAL is an error in Fortran, not a complex value.

title: EXTERNAL declares a procedure passed as an actual argument
legacy:
EXTERNAL FUN
      DOUBLE PRECISION FUN, R
      CALL TRAPZ(FUN, 0.0D0, 1.0D0, 100, R)
notes: EXTERNAL tells the compiler that FUN is a procedure, not a variable; in Python no declaration is needed and the function object is passed directly. TRAPZ assigns its result argument R, so it returns it and the caller stores it. An EXTERNAL name that equals an intrinsic name refers to the user routine, not the intrinsic.

title: INTRINSIC to pass SIN or COS as an argument
legacy:
INTRINSIC SIN, COS
      CALL TABLE(SIN, 0.5, Y1)
      CALL TABLE(COS, 0.5, Y2)
modern:
y1 = table(math.sin, 0.5, y1)
y2 = table(math.cos, 0.5, y2)
notes: An intrinsic function may be an actual argument only if it is named in an INTRINSIC statement, and type conversions (INT, REAL, DBLE ...), lexical comparisons (LGE ...) and MAX and MIN may not be passed; SIN and COS (REAL) and DSIN and DCOS (DOUBLE PRECISION) may. Pass the matching math function, or numpy.sin when it is applied to arrays, and use the same type as the Fortran specific name.

title: Statement function sees current values of the unit's variables
modern:
a = 2.0
b = 1.0


def f(x):
    return a * x + b


y = f(3.0)
a = 4.0
z = f(3.0)
notes: A statement function is a local one-line function whose non-dummy names are the variables of the enclosing unit at the moment of each call, so Y is 7.0 and Z is 13.0. A nested def (or lambda) that reads the enclosing variables behaves the same way; do not bind a and b as default arguments, which would freeze their values.

title: Statement function calling an earlier statement function
legacy:
SQ(T) = T * T
      HYP(P, Q) = SQRT(SQ(P) + SQ(Q))
      H = HYP(3.0, 4.0)
notes: A statement function may use statement functions defined before it, intrinsics and ordinary variables, but not itself. Each becomes a small def placed where the original statement was (before the first executable statement), and the dummy names are local to it, so they never clash with variables of the same name in the unit.

title: Statement function whose name is implicitly INTEGER
notes: The value of a statement function is converted to the type of its name. NR starts with N, so it is INTEGER and the result 3.5 is truncated to 3. Without the int_ conversion the Python function would return 3.5 and every later integer operation on K (division, array subscripts) would be wrong.

title: Triple loop over 2-D arrays keeps its subscript order
legacy:
DO 30 J = 1, M
         DO 20 L = 1, K
            DO 10 I = 1, N
               C(I, J) = C(I, J) + A(I, L) * B(L, J)
   10       CONTINUE
   20    CONTINUE
   30 CONTINUE
notes: A(I,J) becomes a[i - 1, j - 1] with the same order of subscripts; the numpy array has the declared extents (a.shape == (n, k) here) and its memory order is irrelevant to this code. Replacing the loops by a matrix product on slices is valid, but it changes the order of the floating-point summation, so results can differ in the last bits.

title: Whole-array WRITE goes in column-major order
legacy:
REAL A(2, 3)
      WRITE(6, '(3F6.1)') A
modern: write_formatted(6, "(3F6.1)", *a.ravel(order="F"))
notes: An array name without subscripts in an I/O list stands for all its elements in storage order, first subscript fastest. For a = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]] the output is the two lines '   1.0   4.0   2.0' and '   5.0   3.0   6.0'. a.ravel() with the default C order would print 1, 2, 3 first, which is wrong; order="F" gives the Fortran order whatever the array's memory layout.

title: Implied-DO output list runs row by row
modern:
values = [a[i - 1, j - 1] for i in range(1, 3) for j in range(1, 4)]
write_formatted(6, "(3F6.1)", *values)
notes: The inner implied-DO (over J) varies fastest, so the elements come out row by row: '   1.0   2.0   3.0' then '   4.0   5.0   6.0' for a = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]. The comprehension keeps the order of the loops explicit and works when the array is larger than the printed 2 x 3 part, where a plain a.ravel() would not.

title: Array dimensioned A(0:N)
legacy:
SUBROUTINE SQUARES(A, N)
      INTEGER N
      REAL A(0:N)
      DO 10 I = 0, N
         A(I) = REAL(I) ** 2
   10 CONTINUE
      RETURN
      END
notes: A(0:N) has N + 1 elements and Fortran index I is the Python index I - 0, so the subscript is used unchanged and the caller must pass an array of length n + 1. The array is modified in place, nothing is returned. The loop runs to N inclusive (stop n + 1), unlike the usual 1-based loop.

title: Negative and non-unit lower bounds in several dimensions
notes: The extent of each dimension is upper - lower + 1 (H has 5 elements, G is 4 x 3) and every subscript has its own lower bound subtracted. A negative Python index never raises for small values (h[-2] is the fourth element), so a forgotten shift silently reads the wrong element instead of failing; apply the offset in every access.

title: Offset subscripts of arrays with different lower bounds
legacy:
SUBROUTINE DIFF(U, N, H, D)
      INTEGER N
      REAL U(0:N), D(N), H
      DO 10 I = 1, N
         D(I) = (U(I) - U(I - 1)) / H
   10 CONTINUE
      RETURN
      END
notes: U has lower bound 0, so U(I) is u[i] and U(I-1) is u[i - 1], while D has lower bound 1, so D(I) is d[i - 1]; the same loop index shifts differently per array. U has n + 1 elements and D has n. D is the output array, modified in place, so nothing is returned.

title: Adjustable dummy array A(LDA, N)
legacy:
SUBROUTINE SCALE(A, LDA, M, N, S)
      INTEGER LDA, M, N
      REAL A(LDA, N), S
      DO 20 J = 1, N
         DO 10 I = 1, M
            A(I, J) = S * A(I, J)
   10    CONTINUE
   20 CONTINUE
      RETURN
      END
notes: The array extents come from the dummy arguments, but the loops must use M and N (not a.shape), because the caller may pass an array larger than the m x n part that is processed; LDA is the declared leading dimension and is kept as an unused parameter. The array is modified in place. The vectorised form is a[:m, :n] *= s.

title: Work array dimensioned from an argument
legacy:
SUBROUTINE CSUM(X, N, WORK)
      INTEGER N
      REAL X(N), WORK(2 * N)
      WORK(1) = X(1)
      DO 10 I = 2, N
         WORK(I) = WORK(I - 1) + X(I)
   10 CONTINUE
      RETURN
      END
notes: WORK(2*N) is storage supplied by the caller, so the Python function receives it as an array argument (it is not allocated inside, and its contents belong to the caller afterwards). The array must have at least 2 * n elements even though only the first n are written here. N must be at least 1, because the first statement reads X(1).

title: Local array sized by PARAMETER next to an adjustable dummy
legacy:
SUBROUTINE SMOOTH(Y, N)
      INTEGER N, NMAX
      PARAMETER (NMAX = 1000)
      REAL Y(N), T(NMAX)
      DO 10 I = 2, N - 1
         T(I) = 0.25 * Y(I - 1) + 0.5 * Y(I) + 0.25 * Y(I + 1)
   10 CONTINUE
      DO 20 I = 2, N - 1
         Y(I) = T(I)
   20 CONTINUE
      RETURN
      END
notes: A local array must have constant bounds in Fortran 77, so T gets a fixed capacity NMAX and is allocated inside the function, while Y comes from the caller and is updated in place. DO I = 2, N-1 has the inclusive limit N - 1, so range stops at n. The Fortran code has no check that N is at most NMAX; Python raises IndexError there.

title: Assumed-size dummy A(*) with a separate length
legacy:
REAL FUNCTION VSUM(X, N)
      REAL X(*)
      INTEGER N
      VSUM = 0.0
      DO 10 I = 1, N
         VSUM = VSUM + X(I)
   10 CONTINUE
      RETURN
      END
notes: An assumed-size array has no declared size, so the routine can only know how many elements to use from the separate argument N. Always loop to n; never use len(x) or x.sum(), because the numpy array handed in may be longer than the part the Fortran caller meant.

title: Assumed-size last dimension A(LDA, *)
legacy:
SUBROUTINE COLSUM(A, LDA, M, N, S)
      INTEGER LDA, M, N
      REAL A(LDA, *), S(*)
      DO 20 J = 1, N
         S(J) = 0.0
         DO 10 I = 1, M
            S(J) = S(J) + A(I, J)
   10    CONTINUE
   20 CONTINUE
      RETURN
      END
notes: Only the last dimension may be assumed (*), and Fortran cannot query it, so N says how many columns to process; a.shape[1] is merely what the caller allocated. S is the output array, written in place. In Fortran 77 an assumed-size array may not be used as a whole array (for example in I/O) because its extent is unknown.

title: Passing A(1, J) to a routine expecting a vector
legacy:
SUBROUTINE VSCAL(N, S, X)
      INTEGER N
      REAL S, X(N)
      DO 10 I = 1, N
         X(I) = S * X(I)
   10 CONTINUE
      RETURN
      END
C     in the caller:
      REAL A(10, 5)
      CALL VSCAL(10, 2.0, A(1, J))
notes: An array element passed to an array dummy supplies the start of a sequence in storage order. A(1,J) starts column J, whose 10 elements are contiguous in Fortran, so the Python equivalent is the column slice a[:, j - 1]. A basic slice is a view, so the in-place changes made by vscal reach a for any memory order of a.

title: Passing A(I, J) to start in the middle of a column
legacy: CALL VSCAL(5, 2.0, A(3, J))
notes: With VSCAL as in the previous example, A(3,J) starts the sequence at row 3 of column J, so the callee sees rows 3 to 7: the slice a[2:7, j - 1]. This is a view only as long as the segment stays inside the column (3 + 5 - 1 <= 10); when it would run into the next column, use the flat copy-in/copy-out form.

title: Sequence that runs across columns needs a flat F-order copy
legacy:
REAL A(4, 3)
      CALL VSCAL(6, 2.0, A(3, 1))
modern:
flat = np.array(a.reshape(-1, order="F"))
vscal(6, 2.0, flat[2:8])
a[...] = flat.reshape(a.shape, order="F")
notes: The six elements A(3,1), A(4,1), A(1,2) ... A(4,2) cross a column boundary, so they form the flat column-major elements 2 to 7. a.reshape(-1, order="F") (like ravel(order="F")) is a view only when a is Fortran-contiguous and a copy for ordinary C-ordered arrays, so copy explicitly and write the result back with a[...] = ...; this is correct in both cases.

title: Passing a vector to a dummy declared as a matrix
legacy:
REAL B(6)
      CALL MAT23(B)
modern: mat23(b.reshape(2, 3, order="F"))
notes: The callee declares M(2,3), so it sees the 6 storage elements of B as a 2 x 3 column-major matrix (element M(2,1) is B(2), M(1,2) is B(3)). A one-dimensional contiguous array reshaped with order="F" is a view, so the callee's in-place changes reach b. The reverse direction (a matrix passed to a vector dummy) cannot rely on a view; use the flat copy-in/copy-out form.

title: Scalar output argument returned from a SUBROUTINE
legacy:
SUBROUTINE ADD1(X, Y)
      Y = X + 1.0
      RETURN
      END
notes: Fortran passes by reference, so assigning the dummy Y changes the caller's variable; Python returns the new value instead. One assigned scalar means a bare return value (not a tuple), and the parameter Y stays in the signature even though its incoming value is unused. The caller writes y = add1(x, y).

title: FUNCTION that also assigns its arguments
legacy:
INTEGER FUNCTION NXT(I, ISTAT)
      I = I + 1
      NXT = I * 2
      ISTAT = 0
      RETURN
      END
modern:
def nxt(i, istat):
    i = i + 1
    result = i * 2
    istat = 0
    return result, i, istat
notes: A function returns its result first, then every assigned scalar dummy in parameter order: (nxt, i, istat). I is both read and written, so its incoming value matters and its new value is returned. The caller unpacks all three: k, i, istat = nxt(i, istat). The local holding the result must not reuse the function name when it could be confused with recursion.

title: Output assigned on only some paths
legacy:
SUBROUTINE CLAMP(X, LO, HI, ICLIP)
      ICLIP = 0
      IF (X .LT. LO) THEN
         X = LO
         ICLIP = -1
      ELSE IF (X .GT. HI) THEN
         X = HI
         ICLIP = 1
      END IF
      RETURN
      END
notes: X and ICLIP are the assigned scalars, returned in that order (x, iclip). When X is already in range it is not assigned, and the incoming value comes back unchanged because the Python parameter still holds it. LO and HI are never assigned, so they are not returned.

title: Swapping array elements through a subroutine
legacy:
SUBROUTINE SWAP(X, Y)
      T = X
      X = Y
      Y = T
      RETURN
      END
C     in the caller:
      CALL SWAP(A(I), A(J))
modern:
def swap(x, y):
    t = x
    x = y
    y = t
    return x, y


a[i - 1], a[j - 1] = swap(a[i - 1], a[j - 1])
notes: An array element passed to a scalar dummy is an ordinary scalar argument: pass its value and store the returned values back into the same elements. Only whole arrays are modified in place; never return them. If the actual argument is a constant or an expression there is nothing to store back, so the corresponding output is simply discarded.

title: PROGRAM unit becomes main()
legacy:
PROGRAM MAIN
      N = 5
      WRITE(6, *) 'N =', N
      STOP
      END
notes: The main program becomes main() with the usual guard, and its local variables stay local to main. STOP raises FortranStop even as the last statement, so a caller or test that runs main() must expect that exception (code is None for a plain STOP). Reaching END without a STOP simply returns.

title: Function passed as a dummy procedure
legacy:
SUBROUTINE TRAPZ(F, A, B, N, RES)
      EXTERNAL F
      DOUBLE PRECISION F, A, B, RES, H, S
      INTEGER N
      H = (B - A) / N
      S = 0.5D0 * (F(A) + F(B))
      DO 10 I = 1, N - 1
         S = S + F(A + I * H)
   10 CONTINUE
      RES = S * H
      RETURN
      END
modern:
def trapz(f, a, b, n, res):
    h = (b - a) / n
    s = 0.5 * (f(a) + f(b))
    for i in range(1, n):
        s = s + f(a + i * h)
    res = s * h
    return res
notes: A dummy procedure becomes a callable parameter, and F(A) is a call, not an array element. Callbacks follow the same calling convention as any other function. The loop DO I = 1, N-1 has limit N - 1, so range stops at n; it does not run for N = 1. RES is the only assigned scalar, so it is returned.

title: Dummy subroutine that assigns its arguments
legacy:
SUBROUTINE APPLY(SUB, X, Y)
      EXTERNAL SUB
      REAL X, Y
      CALL SUB(X, Y)
      RETURN
      END
notes: The callable passed as SUB follows the convention too: SUB assigns its second argument, so it returns the new value of Y, and APPLY stores it and returns it as its own output. A test double for SUB must therefore return a value (for example lambda x, y: x * 2.0), not mutate anything.

title: D1MACH for double-precision tolerances
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION D1MACH, EPS, TOL, TINY, HUGE
      EXTERNAL D1MACH
      EPS = D1MACH(4)
      TOL = SQRT(EPS)
      TINY = D1MACH(1)
      HUGE = D1MACH(2)
modern:
eps = d1mach(4)
tol = math.sqrt(eps)
tiny = d1mach(1)
huge = d1mach(2)
notes: D1MACH(i) returns IEEE double constants: (1) smallest positive normalised number 2.2250738585072014e-308, (2) largest 1.7976931348623157e+308, (3) 2**-53 (rounding unit), (4) 2**-52 = 2.220446049250313e-16 (machine epsilon), (5) log10(2). Keep the call (the runtime supplies the values) instead of inlining numbers, and keep the index, since 3 and 4 differ by a factor of two.

title: R1MACH single-precision constants stay single
legacy:
REAL R1MACH, EPS
      EXTERNAL R1MACH
      EPS = R1MACH(4)
      IF (ABS(DELTA) .LT. 10.0 * EPS) ICONV = 1
notes: R1MACH(4) is the single-precision epsilon 2**-23 = 1.1920928955078125e-07 (R1MACH(1) is 1.1754944e-38, R1MACH(2) is 3.4028235e+38, R1MACH(3) is 2**-24). Do not replace it with d1mach: a convergence test against the single-precision epsilon is much looser than one against the double epsilon and changes when the loop stops.

title: I1MACH for unit numbers and the largest integer
legacy:
INTEGER I1MACH, LOUT, IMAX
      EXTERNAL I1MACH
      LOUT = I1MACH(2)
      IMAX = I1MACH(9)
      WRITE(LOUT, '(1X, A, I11)') 'LARGEST INTEGER ', IMAX
modern:
lout = i1mach(2)
imax = i1mach(9)
write_formatted(lout, "(1X,A,I11)", 'LARGEST INTEGER ', imax)
notes: I1MACH(1) is the standard input unit (5), I1MACH(2) the standard output unit (6) and I1MACH(9) the largest 32-bit integer 2147483647. The unit number is a variable here, so it is passed to the runtime as a value; units 5 and 6 map to stdin and stdout. The line prints ' LARGEST INTEGER ' followed by ' 2147483647' (I11 is right-justified).

title: WRITE with a labeled FORMAT statement
modern: write_formatted(6, "(1X,'N =',I4,2X,'X =',F9.3)", n, x)
notes: The FORMAT label is replaced by the format string at the call, and the FORMAT statement is deleted. With n = 12 and x = 3.14159 the record is ' N =  12  X =    3.142'. The first character is not treated as carriage control: the 1X is a real blank in the output, as in gfortran.

title: E, F and I descriptors differ from Python's % formatting
modern:
write_formatted(6, "(E12.4)", x)
write_formatted(6, "(F6.1,I5)", y, k)
notes: E12.4 prints a leading-zero mantissa: 123.456 gives '  0.1235E+03', while Python's '%12.4E' gives '  1.2346E+02'. A value that does not fit the field width is shown as asterisks (F6.1 of 1234567.0 gives '******', I5 of 123456 gives '*****'), whereas Python just widens the field. To get a record as a string instead of printing, use format_record(fmt, values).

title: More list items than descriptors: format reuse
modern: write_formatted(6, "(3F6.1)", *v[:5])
notes: When the I/O list is longer than the format, the format is reused and a new record is started: for v = 1.0 ... 5.0 the output is the two lines '   1.0   2.0   3.0' and '   4.0   5.0'. A slash in a format also ends the record. Every WRITE statement starts a new record, so a WRITE with an empty list prints a blank line.

title: A, Aw and the padding of CHARACTER values
legacy:
CHARACTER*6 NAME
      NAME = 'ALPHA'
      WRITE(6, '(1X, A, 1X, A3, 1X, A8)') NAME, NAME, NAME
modern:
name = char_assign('ALPHA', 6)
write_formatted(6, "(1X,A,1X,A3,1X,A8)", name, name, name)
notes: A without a width prints the whole value including its trailing blank, so the string passed must already be padded to the declared length (6). A3 prints the leftmost 3 characters ('ALP'); A8 is wider than the value, so it right-justifies it, preceded by two blanks. The record is ' ALPHA  ALP   ALPHA '.

title: T, X descriptors place fields by column
modern: write_formatted(6, "(T5,A2,T12,I3,2X,F5.1)", 'AB', 7, 2.5)
notes: Tn moves to absolute column n of the record (1-based) and fills skipped columns with blanks, nX skips n columns relative to the current position. Here 'AB' sits in columns 5 and 6, the integer 7 ends in column 14, and 2.5 occupies columns 17 to 21, giving '    AB       7    2.5'. Columns are positions in the output line, not in the Python string index.

title: Internal files: converting between numbers and strings
legacy:
CHARACTER*10 BUF
      WRITE(BUF, '(I5)') N
      READ(BUF, '(I5)') M
modern:
buf = char_assign(write_internal("(I5)", n), 10)
(m,) = read_internal(buf, "(I5)")
notes: WRITE to a CHARACTER variable formats into the string and pads it with blanks to the variable's length, so BUF for N = 42 is '   42' plus five blanks. READ from the string applies the format to the stored text, so M is 42 again. It is the Fortran idiom for number-to-string and string-to-number conversion; do not replace it with str() and int(), which ignore the field widths.

title: Formatted READ uses fixed-width fields
modern: k, y = read_formatted(5, "(I3,F6.2)")
notes: The record is cut into fields by the format, not by blanks: the line ' 42 12345' gives K = 42 and Y = 123.45, because without a decimal point in the field the last two digits are the fraction; a field written '1.5' keeps its decimal point. An all-blank numeric field reads as zero. Unit 5 is standard input.

title: List-directed PRINT and WRITE(*,*)
legacy:
PRINT *, 'SUM =', S
      WRITE(*, *) N, X
modern:
write_list(6, 'SUM =', s)
write_list(6, n, x)
notes: PRINT * and WRITE(*,*) write to the standard output unit 6. The exact spacing, the number of digits of real values and the leading blank are chosen by the compiler (gfortran starts each record with a blank and uses fixed-width fields), so the runtime only approximates them. Compare such output token by token, not as exact text; use an explicit FORMAT when the layout matters.

title: List-directed READ with free-format input
legacy: READ(5, *) N, X
modern: n, x = read_list(5, 2, [int, float])
notes: Items may be separated by blanks, commas or line ends, and a READ continues onto following lines until all items have values; the rest of the last record read is then skipped. The Fortran type of each item is not visible to the reader, so pass the target types (int for an INTEGER, float for a REAL; the input '4' is a valid REAL value). At end of file read_list raises EOFError.

title: OPEN, READ and CLOSE of a data file
legacy:
OPEN(UNIT=10, FILE='data.dat', STATUS='OLD')
      READ(10, *) N
      READ(10, *) (X(I), I = 1, N)
      CLOSE(10)
modern:
open_unit(10, file="data.dat", status="old")
(n,) = read_list(10, 1, int)
x[:n] = read_list(10, n, float)
close_unit(10)
notes: Each READ starts at a new record, so N is taken from the first line and the N values of the implied-DO list from the following ones (possibly several lines). STATUS='OLD' requires the file to exist. Units 5 and 6 are preconnected to standard input and output and are never opened. Names given in OPEN are relative to the working directory.

title: Scratch file with REWIND
legacy:
OPEN(UNIT=11, STATUS='SCRATCH')
      WRITE(11, *) A, B
      REWIND 11
      READ(11, *) C, D
      CLOSE(11)
modern:
open_unit(11, status="scratch")
write_list(11, a, b)
rewind_unit(11)
c, d = read_list(11, 2, float)
close_unit(11)
notes: A SCRATCH file has no name and is deleted when it is closed or the program ends. REWIND repositions the unit at the start of the file so what was written can be read back. ENDFILE writes an end-of-file mark (endfile_unit). C and D are REAL targets, so the list-directed values are read as float.

title: READ with END= loops until end of file
legacy:
N = 0
      TOTAL = 0.0
   10 READ(10, *, END=20) X
      N = N + 1
      TOTAL = TOTAL + X
      GO TO 10
   20 CONTINUE
notes: END=label is taken when the READ meets end of file; the runtime raises EOFError, which becomes the exit from the loop. Wrap only the READ in try/except so that other errors are not hidden. The items of the failed READ are undefined afterwards (X is not usable after the loop), and the same pattern replaces ERR= and IOSTAT= branches for other read errors.

title: BACKSPACE to read the same record twice
legacy:
CHARACTER*1 C
      READ(10, '(A1)') C
      BACKSPACE 10
      IF (C .EQ. 'X') READ(10, '(A1, I4)') C, K
modern:
(c,) = read_formatted(10, "(A1)")
backspace_unit(10)
if str_eq(c, 'X'):
    c, k = read_formatted(10, "(A1,I4)")
notes: BACKSPACE moves back to the start of the record just read, so the second READ sees the same line with a different format (here the first character is used as a record type). C is CHARACTER*1, so it is compared with str_eq, which ignores trailing blanks. The first READ consumes one record even though it takes a single character.

title: INQUIRE has no runtime helper
legacy:
LOGICAL EX
      INQUIRE(FILE='cfg.dat', EXIST=EX)
      IF (.NOT. EX) STOP 1
notes: There is no f77rt helper for INQUIRE; use os.path or pathlib (trailing blanks in a FILE= value are ignored by Fortran, so strip them from a padded CHARACTER variable). A unit that is written without an OPEN is implicitly connected by gfortran to a file named fort.N (fort.12 for unit 12), which is easy to miss when porting.

title: Hollerith constants in FORMAT and as arguments
legacy:
WRITE(6, 10)
   10 FORMAT(5HHELLO, 1X, 5HWORLD)
      CALL MSG(5HHELLO)
modern:
write_formatted(6, "('HELLO',1X,'WORLD')")
msg('HELLO')
notes: nHtext means the n characters after the H, blanks included, so 5HHELLO is the string 'HELLO'. Convert it to an ordinary quoted string literal, and pass strings where the callee expects a character argument. A wrong count in the original silently shifts or swallows characters; count again rather than trusting the text.

title: Hollerith data stored in integer arrays
legacy:
INTEGER ITITLE(3)
      DATA ITITLE /4HABCD, 4HEFGH, 4HIJKL/
      WRITE(6, 20) ITITLE
   20 FORMAT(1X, 3A4)
modern:
title = ['ABCD', 'EFGH', 'IJKL']
write_formatted(6, "(1X,3A4)", *title)
notes: Old programs packed four characters into each default INTEGER and printed them with A4. Python integers cannot hold the text, so store a list of 4-character strings (a shorter Hollerith is padded with blanks). This is valid only if the integer values are never used arithmetically or compared as numbers; otherwise flag it.

title: Continuation lines and comment lines
legacy:
C     SUM OF SEVEN TERMS
      TOTAL = A(1) + A(2) + A(3) + A(4) + A(5)
     +        + A(6) + A(7)
      WRITE(6, 100) 'TOTAL = ',
     &              TOTAL
  100 FORMAT(1X, A, F8.2)
modern:
# SUM OF SEVEN TERMS
total = (a[0] + a[1] + a[2] + a[3] + a[4]
         + a[5] + a[6])
write_formatted(6, "(1X,A,F8.2)", 'TOTAL = ', total)
notes: A nonblank, nonzero character in column 6 marks a continuation of the previous line (up to 19 continuation lines); the character itself is not part of the statement. A C or * in column 1 is a comment, which may even sit between continuation lines. Blanks are not significant outside character constants. Python needs parentheses (or a backslash) to continue an expression.

title: Text after column 72 is ignored
legacy:
TOTAL = ALPHA1 + ALPHA2 + ALPHA3 + ALPHA4 + ALPHA5 + ALPHA6 + A7
     +        + B8
modern:
total = (alpha1 + alpha2 + alpha3 + alpha4 + alpha5 + alpha6 + a7
         + b8)
notes: Columns 73 to 80 are not part of a statement (they once held card sequence numbers). A line that runs past column 72 is silently cut: if the first line here ended at column 74 the last characters would be lost and, say, a name could become a different variable. Check the original source for non-blank text beyond column 72 and report it rather than silently completing the statement.

title: Blanks are ignored, so DO 10 I = 1.5 is an assignment
legacy:
DO 10 I = 1.5
      X = X + 1.0
   10 CONTINUE
notes: Outside character constants blanks have no meaning and keywords are not reserved, so with a period instead of the comma the first statement is the assignment DO10I = 1.5 to an implicitly typed REAL variable; it is not a loop and the other two statements run once. Check for a comma before treating a DO as a loop. Likewise GOTO equals GO TO and ENDIF equals END IF.

title: Integer division truncates toward zero
modern:
i = idiv(7, 2)
j = idiv(-7, 2)
k = idiv(7, -2)
l = idiv(-7, -2)
notes: The results are 3, -3, -3 and 3. Python's // rounds toward minus infinity and gives -4 for the second and third; int(a / b) goes through floating point and can lose precision for large operands. Use idiv for every integer division unless both operands are known to be non-negative.

title: Mixed-mode expressions: where the truncation happens
modern:
y = idiv(1, 2) * x
z = x * idiv(1, 2)
w = 1.0 / 2 * x
r = float(idiv(n, m))
notes: Operators of equal precedence group left to right, and an operation on two integers is an integer operation: 1 / 2 is 0, so Y and Z are 0.0 and only W is 0.5 * X. R is a REAL variable but receives the already truncated quotient (n = 7, m = 2 gives 3.0). Never turn integer / integer into Python's true division.

title: Integer exponentiation, including negative exponents
modern:
i = ipow(2, -1)
j = ipow(-2, 3)
k = ipow(2, ipow(3, 2))
l = ipow(-1, -3)
notes: An integer raised to a negative integer power is evaluated as 1 / (base ** |exp|) in integer arithmetic, so I = 0, and L = -1; Python's 2 ** -1 gives the float 0.5. Exponentiation groups right to left (K = 2 ** 9 = 512), like Python, and -2 ** 2 means -(2 ** 2). Integer overflow wraps in practice in Fortran, never in Python.

title: Ceiling division for blocks and an odd test with MOD
legacy:
NB = (N + NSIZE - 1) / NSIZE
      DO 10 IB = 1, NB
         ILO = (IB - 1) * NSIZE + 1
         IHI = MIN(IB * NSIZE, N)
         CALL WORK(ILO, IHI)
   10 CONTINUE
      IF (MOD(N, 2) .EQ. 1) K = K + 1
modern:
nb = idiv(n + nsize - 1, nsize)
for ib in range(1, nb + 1):
    ilo = (ib - 1) * nsize + 1
    ihi = min(ib * nsize, n)
    work(ilo, ihi)
if fmod(n, 2) == 1:
    k = k + 1
notes: With N = 10 and NSIZE = 4, NB = 13 / 4 = 3 blocks (1-4, 5-8, 9-10). MOD(N, 2) .EQ. 1 is true only for positive odd N because MOD(-3, 2) is -1, while Python's -3 % 2 is 1; translate MOD with fmod to keep that behaviour. The loop runs max(NB, 0) times, so a non-positive N skips it.

title: MOD, AMOD, DMOD take the sign of the first argument
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION D
      I = MOD(-7, 3)
      J = MOD(7, -3)
      X = AMOD(-7.5, 2.0)
      D = DMOD(5.5D0, -2.0D0)
notes: MOD(A, P) = A - INT(A / P) * P, so the results are -1, 1, -1.5 and 1.5. Python's % takes the sign of the divisor and gives 2, -2, 0.5 and -0.5. For floating point the runtime uses math.fmod, which is also what gfortran computes. P must not be zero. fmod keeps integer arguments integer, unlike math.fmod, which always returns a float.

title: SIGN and ISIGN transfer the sign of the second argument
notes: SIGN(A, B) is |A| when B >= 0 and -|A| when B < 0, giving -3.0, 3.0, 3.0 and -5. It is not the sign function of A. math.copysign always returns a float, so it is wrong for ISIGN (copysign(5, -2) is -5.0, which is no longer an integer), and abs(a) * (1 if b >= 0 else -1) is easy to get wrong for zero.

title: NINT rounds halves away from zero
legacy:
I = NINT(2.5)
      J = NINT(-2.5)
      K = NINT(2.4)
      X = ANINT(-0.5)
      L = INT(-2.7 + 0.5)
      M = NINT(-2.7)
modern:
i = nint(2.5)
j = nint(-2.5)
k = nint(2.4)
x = anint(-0.5)
l = int_(-2.7 + 0.5)
m = nint(-2.7)
notes: The results are 3, -3, 2, -1.0, -2 and -3. Python's round(2.5) is 2 because it rounds halves to even (numpy.round does too). The hand-written rounding INT(X + 0.5) is not NINT for negative numbers (L is -2, M is -3), so keep such code as int_(x + 0.5) rather than replacing it with round.

title: INT, AINT and IFIX truncate toward zero
legacy:
I = INT(-2.7)
      X = AINT(-2.7)
      J = INT(2.9)
      K = IFIX(-0.5)
notes: The results are -2, -2.0, 2 and 0. INT keeps the integer part, so it differs from math.floor for negative arguments (floor(-2.7) is -3); AINT does the same but returns a REAL. Python's int() truncates too, but int_ is the uniform replacement for INT, IFIX and IDINT, and aint and anint cover the REAL-valued forms.

title: DIM keeps the argument type; MAX and MIN take any number of arguments
notes: DIM(A, B) is A - B when A > B and zero otherwise: 2.0, 0.0 and 0. max(a - b, 0) is wrong for REAL arguments because it returns the integer 0 on the zero branch and loses the type. Fortran 77 requires all arguments of MAX and MIN to have the same type, and AMIN1 and MAX0 are the typed specific versions.

title: DABS, DSQRT, DEXP and other DOUBLE PRECISION names
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION X, Y, Z
      Y = DABS(X) + DSQRT(X) + DEXP(X) + DLOG(X) + DLOG10(X)
      Z = DSIN(X) * DCOS(X) + DATAN2(Y, X) + DMAX1(X, Y, Z)
modern:
y = abs(x) + math.sqrt(x) + math.exp(x) + math.log(x) + math.log10(x)
z = math.sin(x) * math.cos(x) + math.atan2(y, x) + max(x, y, z)
notes: The D prefix only selects the DOUBLE PRECISION version, so these map to the plain Python or math functions. Error cases differ: math.sqrt of a negative and math.log of zero or a negative raise ValueError where Fortran yields NaN or -Infinity; the tests should only cover well-defined inputs. DMAX1 and DMIN1 accept any number of arguments.

title: FLOAT, IFIX, AMAX0, MIN1, SNGL and DBLE
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION D
      X = FLOAT(N) / 2.0
      K = IFIX(X)
      R = AMAX0(I, J, K)
      L = MIN1(2.7, 3.5, 9.1)
      D = DBLE(I) / 2
      S = SNGL(D)
modern:
x = float(n) / 2.0
k = int_(x)
r = float(max(i, j, k))
l = int_(min(2.7, 3.5, 9.1))
d = float(i) / 2
s = float(np.float32(d))
notes: The old specific names fix both argument and result types: AMAX0 takes integers and returns a REAL, MIN1 takes reals and returns an INTEGER by truncation (L is 2, not 3), IFIX is INT for a REAL, FLOAT converts an integer and DBLE or SNGL change precision. D = DBLE(I) / 2 is a real division because 2 is converted to double.

title: IABS, MAX0, ISIGN, ALOG, ALOG10, DPROD and CABS
legacy:
DOUBLE PRECISION D
      COMPLEX Z
      K = IABS(I) + MAX0(I, J) + ISIGN(I, J)
      X = ALOG(Y) + ALOG10(Y) + AMOD(Y, 2.0)
      D = DPROD(A, B)
      R = CABS(Z)
modern:
k = abs(i) + max(i, j) + sign(i, j)
x = math.log(y) + math.log10(y) + fmod(y, 2.0)
d = float(a) * float(b)
r = abs(z)
notes: ALOG is the natural logarithm (math.log), ALOG10 the base-10 one, IABS and CABS are abs for integers and complex numbers, and ISIGN and AMOD need the Fortran-semantics helpers (sign, fmod). DPROD multiplies two REAL values in double precision, so the product is exact; the converted code multiplies as doubles.

title: IAND, IOR, IEOR and NOT on 32-bit integers
legacy:
J = IAND(I, 255)
      K = IOR(J, 256)
      L = IEOR(K, 15)
      M = NOT(I)
modern:
j = iand(i, 255)
k = ior(j, 256)
l = ieor(k, 15)
m = not_(i)
notes: These operate on the bits of a default (32-bit, two's complement) INTEGER, so NOT(5) is -6 and IAND(-1, 255) is 255. Python's &, |, ^ and ~ agree for values within 32 bits, but Python integers do not wrap and have no fixed width, so use the helpers to keep the results in the 32-bit range.

title: ISHFT is a logical shift in both directions
legacy:
I = ISHFT(1, 4)
      J = ISHFT(16, -4)
      K = ISHFT(-1, -1)
      L = ISHFT(1, 31)
modern:
i = ishft(1, 4)
j = ishft(16, -4)
k = ishft(-1, -1)
l = ishft(1, 31)
notes: A positive count shifts left and a negative count shifts right with zero fill, and bits shifted out are lost: the results are 16, 1, 2147483647 and -2147483648. Python's -1 >> 1 is -1 (arithmetic shift) and 1 << 31 is 2147483648, so neither operator is a substitute. Shift counts of 32 or more are processor-dependent.

title: BTEST, IBSET and IBCLR expressed with masks
legacy:
IF (BTEST(I, 3)) K = K + 1
      I = IBSET(I, 5)
      I = IBCLR(I, 0)
modern:
if iand(i, ishft(1, 3)) != 0:
    k = k + 1
i = ior(i, ishft(1, 5))
i = iand(i, not_(ishft(1, 0)))
notes: BTEST, IBSET, IBCLR, IBITS and ISHFTC, like IAND, IOR, IEOR, NOT and ISHFT, are MIL-STD-1753 or vendor extensions, not Fortran 77 standard intrinsics; express the first three with masks. Bits are numbered from 0 at the least significant end, and bit 31 is the sign bit, so ishft(1, 31) is negative. Build the mask with ishft and combine it with iand, ior and not_.

title: Dotted relational and logical operators
legacy:
LOGICAL FLAG
      IF (X .GE. 0.0 .AND. X .LE. 1.0 .OR. .NOT. FLAG) K = 1
      IF (I .NE. J) L = 1
notes: .EQ. .NE. .LT. .LE. .GT. .GE. map to == != < <= > >=, and .AND. .OR. .NOT. to and, or, not. The precedence is the same in both languages: relational operators bind tighter than .NOT., which binds tighter than .AND., which binds tighter than .OR.; the parentheses added here only make that explicit. Compare CHARACTER operands with the string helpers, not with these operators.

title: .EQV. and .NEQV. need parentheses in Python
legacy:
LOGICAL P, Q, R
      R = P .EQV. Q
      IF (A .GT. 0.0 .EQV. B .GT. 0.0) K = 1
      IF (P .AND. Q .NEQV. R) L = 1
notes: .EQV. and .NEQV. have the lowest precedence of all logical operators, so each side is a complete logical or relational expression. Always parenthesise both operands in Python: a > 0.0 == b > 0.0 is a chained comparison meaning (a > 0.0) and (0.0 == b) and (b > 0.0), and p and q != r groups differently from (p and q) != r.

title: Compound condition that guards an array access
legacy: IF (I .LE. N .AND. A(I) .GT. 0.0) K = K + 1
notes: Fortran may evaluate both operands, so the original test is only safe if A(I) is readable when I > N. Python's and short-circuits, which is harmless here. The translation also checks 1 <= i, because a[i - 1] with i = 0 would silently read the last element instead of failing. Do not rely on short-circuiting if the second operand is a function call with side effects.

title: Substring A(i:j) is 1-based and inclusive
legacy:
CHARACTER*10 S
      CHARACTER*3 T
      CHARACTER*1 C
      CHARACTER*4 U, V
      S = 'ABCDEFGHIJ'
      T = S(3:5)
      C = S(7:7)
      U = S(:4)
      V = S(8:)
modern:
s = char_assign('ABCDEFGHIJ', 10)
t = char_assign(substr(s, 3, 5), 3)
c = char_assign(substr(s, 7, 7), 1)
u = char_assign(s[:4], 4)
v = char_assign(s[7:], 4)
notes: Both bounds are included: S(3:5) is 'CDE' and S(7:7) is 'G'. An omitted lower bound means 1 and an omitted upper bound means LEN(S), so U is 'ABCD' and V is 'HIJ' padded to 'HIJ ' by the assignment. Python slices shift by one (s[2:5]) and silently clip out-of-range bounds, which Fortran treats as an error; substr keeps the Fortran numbering.

title: Assigning to a substring
legacy:
CHARACTER*10 S
      S = 'ABCDEFGHIJ'
      S(2:4) = 'XY'
      S(8:9) = 'PQRS'
modern:
s = char_assign('ABCDEFGHIJ', 10)
s = set_substr(s, 2, 4, 'XY')
s = set_substr(s, 8, 9, 'PQRS')
notes: The value assigned to S(i:j) is padded or truncated to the substring length j - i + 1: S(2:4) = 'XY' stores 'XY ' and S(8:9) = 'PQRS' stores 'PQ', leaving the rest of S untouched; the result is 'AXY EFGPQJ'. Python strings are immutable, so the new string is built and rebound; the total length never changes.

title: Concatenation keeps the blank padding of CHARACTER*n
legacy:
CHARACTER*8 FIRST, LAST
      CHARACTER*17 FULL
      FIRST = 'ANN'
      LAST = 'LEE'
      FULL = FIRST // ' ' // LAST
modern:
first = char_assign('ANN', 8)
last = char_assign('LEE', 8)
full = char_assign(first + ' ' + last, 17)
notes: FIRST is 'ANN' followed by five blanks, so the concatenation is 8 + 1 + 8 = 17 characters: 'ANN', six blanks, then 'LEE' and five more blanks. The padding is part of the value, so the variables must be padded on assignment; with unpadded Python strings the result would be 'ANN LEE'. To remove the padding, take FIRST(1:LEN_TRIM(FIRST)).

title: ICHAR, CHAR and INDEX
legacy:
CHARACTER*1 C
      N = ICHAR('A')
      C = CHAR(N + 1)
      K = INDEX('ABCDEF', 'CD')
      L = INDEX('ABCDEF', 'X')
modern:
n = ichar('A')
c = char_(n + 1)
k = index_('ABCDEF', 'CD')
l = index_('ABCDEF', 'X')
notes: ICHAR returns the position in the character set (65 for 'A' in ASCII) and CHAR is its inverse. INDEX returns the 1-based position of the first match, 3 here, and 0 when the substring is absent, whereas Python's str.find is 0-based and returns -1. The helper index_ keeps the Fortran numbering.

title: CHARACTER dummy modified one character at a time
legacy:
SUBROUTINE UPCASE(S)
      CHARACTER*(*) S
      DO 10 I = 1, LEN(S)
         IC = ICHAR(S(I:I))
         IF (IC .GE. 97 .AND. IC .LE. 122) S(I:I) = CHAR(IC - 32)
   10 CONTINUE
      RETURN
      END
notes: Strings are immutable, so a CHARACTER dummy that the routine assigns (here through substring assignment) is an output and the new string is returned; the length does not change. The caller writes s = upcase(s). The code assumes the ASCII character set, which is what gfortran uses.

title: LLT, LGE and ordering of CHARACTER values
legacy:
IF (LLT(A, B)) K = 1
      IF (LGE(A, 'M')) L = 1
notes: LLT, LLE, LGT and LGE compare with the ASCII collating sequence (digits before upper-case letters before lower-case letters) and pad the shorter operand with blanks, so trailing blanks never matter. Python's < on str compares without that padding. Plain .LT. on CHARACTER operands is the same comparison on ASCII systems and is converted with str_cmp.

title: DO WHILE ... END DO
legacy:
DO WHILE (ERR .GT. TOL)
         ERR = ERR / 2.0
         N = N + 1
      END DO
notes: DO WHILE is not Fortran 77 but is accepted by nearly every compiler. The condition is tested before each iteration, including the first, so the body may run zero times, and there is no loop variable. If the body never makes the condition false, both versions loop forever.

title: DO ... END DO with EXIT and CYCLE
legacy:
DO I = 1, N
         IF (A(I) .LT. 0.0) CYCLE
         IF (A(I) .GT. 99.0) EXIT
         S = S + A(I)
      END DO
notes: A DO without a statement label, closed by END DO, is the same loop as a labeled one; CYCLE is continue and EXIT is break. After EXIT the index keeps the current value; after normal completion it is 1 + max(n, 0), which a Python for loop does not reproduce, so set it explicitly if it is used later.

title: INCLUDE of a shared declaration file
legacy:
SUBROUTINE STEP
      INCLUDE 'ctl.inc'
      NSTEP = NSTEP + 1
      RETURN
      END
C     ctl.inc contains:  COMMON /CTL/ NSTEP
modern:
from types import SimpleNamespace

# INCLUDE 'ctl.inc' (contains COMMON /CTL/ NSTEP)
ctl = SimpleNamespace(nstep=0)


def step():
    ctl.nstep = ctl.nstep + 1
notes: INCLUDE inserts the text of another file at that point, so the declarations it contains apply as if written there. The converted module must be self-contained: expand the included declarations, create the shared COMMON state object only once at module level (not per unit that includes it), and report the include as unresolved if its content is not available instead of guessing names.

title: STRUCTURE and RECORD (DEC extension)
legacy:
STRUCTURE /POINT/
         REAL X, Y
      END STRUCTURE
      RECORD /POINT/ P
      P.X = 1.0
      P.Y = P.X + 2.0
modern:
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Point:
    x: float = 0.0
    y: float = 0.0


p = Point()
p.x = 1.0
p.y = p.x + 2.0
notes: A STRUCTURE declaration defines a record type and RECORD creates a variable of it; fields are accessed with a dot. A dataclass is the natural equivalent, with defaults matching the field types. NAMELIST is another extension without a runtime helper; read such input by a small explicit parser or flag it as unsupported.

title: %VAL, %REF and %LOC argument qualifiers
legacy: CALL CSUB(%VAL(N), %REF(X))
modern:
# %VAL(N) passes N by value, %REF(X) by reference
x = csub(n, x)
notes: These qualifiers control how arguments reach non-Fortran code such as C routines; scalars are already passed by value in Python. If CSUB is a C or system routine its source is not part of the Fortran file, so supply a Python implementation or report it as unresolved. Assuming CSUB assigns X through the reference, it returns the new value that must be stored back.
